parimitameva | evaṃ saṃsāriṇi kramavikāso yāvat sarvajñeṣu vikāsatāratamyena, paramo vikāso rudrabhuvi śūnyasya | tadāha sarvabhāva iti | tat iti cittattvam | ivaśabdena vāstavo na ko'pi saṅkocastadābhāsamātraṃ muktveti darśayati tathāpi iti saṅkoce'pi | evaṃ śūnyasya antargatatattadvastunyūnatādhikyakṛtaṃ saṅkocavikāsatāratamyamiti uktvā tadā sarvāvaraṇalope tasya jñānasya ānantyāt jñeyamalpamityanayā dṛṣṭyā jñeyasaṃskāravicchedatāratamyena saṃvidbhāgavikāsāt vikāsatāratamyaṃ grāhyagrāhakabhāvotthāpakamiti darśayati yogināṃ ca iti naca anastheti smārayati tasya tu iti | śūnyāntare vedyāt śūnyādasya viṣeśaṃ tunā āha | evaṃ samāveśopadeśaśūnyānāṃ pratiyogisaṃvalitameva niṣedhameva buddhyamānānāmabuddhānāmanantasṛjyamānaśūnyayogo yogināmiti uktam | ye tu samāveśaviśāradāstattvavidaste dehādimeva yadyapi bodharūpāviṣṭamabhimanyante, tathāpi taddehaprāṇādibhedollāsanopayoginā śūnyena avaśyamantarā bhāvyaṃ, natu tatra śūnyāntareṇa kiñcidityetat darśayati pāramārthikapakṣāntaraparigraheṇa yadivā iti | viśeṣābhāvāt iti ghaṭena yā śūnyatā neti bhāti, yā ca ghaṭapaṭābhyāṃ; tatra pratiyogibhedaṃ (page 379) muktvā na svarūpato bhedo vivekavatāmavabhātīti na śūnyāntaraṃ kiñcidasti | nanu evaṃ saṃsāriṇāṃ yogabhuvi śūnyasaṃvedanaṃ kena, nahi teṣāmaiśvarī saṃvidasti | ka evamāha, astyeva sā | tadāha sarvā caiṣā iti | pratipāditam iti pūrvaḥ pūrva uttaramuttaraṃ vyabhicarati, natu uttaraḥ pūrvamiti hi uktam | tatra iti tasyāṃ pramātṛparamparāyām | madhye raudra iti so'pi māyīyatvena heyaḥ | tathāpi na heyaḥ ityāha sa tu iti | evaṃ śūnyapramātṛsvarūpaṃ pradarśya vṛttiṃ vyācaṣṭe atra iti | kṣetraśabdena śarīraṃ vadatā tacchūnyānāṃ na asti vikalpanaśaktiriti uktam | apohyamāna iti saṃvidamapekṣya yā vikalpanaśaktiḥ, sā bhedadṛṣṭyā tattvarūpatāmāpannā mano'ntaḥkaraṇam | tacca pratiyogyapohanasahitārthāvamarśanavyāpāram | tatraiva ca rūḍhatā saṃsāritā, tata eva paścādapohaprakaraṇaṃ sambandhastu śaktisparśa iti bodhābodhātmā pramātā paramārthapramātari
**The bond and the liberation: how the bound creates, and how he is freed** We come now to the heart of the matter: the essence of the knower, the known, the bond, and the liberation. The great question is how the bound knower relates to the Lord. For the bound one does not merely suffer the world; he *creates* it, after his own fashion. But his creation is not the Lord's. The bound one's creation is *un-common* (asādhāraṇī) — it is private, his own, per-knower and per-moment, vanishing with him. Yet it does not stand on its own: it is *sustained by the Lord's creation* (īśasṛṣṭyujīvinī), riding on the back of the reality that the Lord alone makes. The objection arises: "if the paśu creates, is his creation not common, like the Lord's?" No. The paśu's own power is hidden from him — he is other-dependent — and only the Lord-ness can awaken it. The whole difference of bound and liberated hangs on a single fact: the bound one does not *know* his own power. He forgets that the world he builds is built with the Lord's own materials. The māyā-power, the word-mass of the Lord, the wheel of the syllable-deities, the eight-fold class — all this moves through him like the rising and falling of the breath, and makes the "friend-this, enemy-this" constructions of his little world. Even his wildest creations — the ten-tusked elephant of his fancy — are only rearrangements of appearances the Lord has made. The construction-action, then, is the bond. It is of the breath-form, ever-moving, and it exists precisely to obstruct the bound one's rest. By it the māyā-power binds the animal. Even the seemingly free constructions — "I, the king, stand," "I have slain my enemy" — are, on inspection, other- dependent; the bound one's freedom is only apparent, resting on the Lord's. And this is the māyā in its threefold working: the appearance of the void, the appearance of the opposite, the mere negation — all spreading through the three stains. Against this stands the Lord's own creation. It is *common* (sādhāraṇā) and clear-manifestation — never constructed, always whole. And there is a path out of the bound one's prison: the abandonment of construction. When, by the thinning of the constructions and the gathering of the mind to one point, the bound one comes to the "I-this" of the Lord, his animal-ness is destroyed and the Lord-ness shines. Even the animal's own creation, if it is known in the light of the Lord's power, becomes common and real. The whole practice — the one-pointedness, the cultivation — is the letting-go of the constructions that bind. And this is the recognition. The world-self — the very one who is the grasper and the grasped, the manifestation and its mass — that one is the "I." The Lord is not another; he is the "aham" of every "aham." When the constructions fall into the great re-recollection, they cease to construct; they become the non-construction, the pure recognition. The bound one sees that he was never bound — that all along he was the Lord, playing at finitude as a king plays at being a soldier. What, then, of the known? The known — the objects of the world — is common: the same for the bound and the liberated. But they know it differently. The liberated one knows it *with the non-difference of his own self*: he knows the whole knower-group, from the pure realm down to the embryo, as "I-this," one flavor, un-divided. The bound one knows it in the reversal, as utterly other, divided into things. The known is the same; the knowing is not. But in the supreme Śiva — the highest — there is no separate known at all. In the pure realm there is a known-order; in the while-living-liberated there is; but in the parama-Śiva, the "I"-experience is filled and nothing stands over against it. It is the consciousness-bliss-mass, the supreme, beyond all syllables. There is no object there, because there is no otherness there. And the fruit of the whole teaching is this: knowing one's own self as the Lord-form, seeing the knowled
